passage: Producing a single ukiyo-e woodblock print in Edo-period Japan was rarely the work of one person. A publisher commissioned the design and financed the project; an artist supplied a master drawing; a carver pasted that drawing onto a block of cherry wood and cut away everything that was not to be inked; and a printer, working from a separate block for each color, pressed the sheet by hand against one block after another, aligning it each time against small marks cut into the wood. The names that survive on the prints are almost always the artist's and the publisher's. The carvers and printers, whose skill determined whether a delicate gradation of sky or water came out cleanly, are in most cases anonymous.
question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It traces the steady rise in the market value of ukiyo-e woodblock prints from the Edo period through to the present day.
It argues that a few celebrated print designers have unfairly overshadowed the rival designers who worked in the same period.
It describes the division of labor behind a woodblock print and then observes that credit for the finished work was distributed unequally.
It explains the chemical process by which the colored inks used in Japanese woodblock printing were manufactured and prepared.

explanation: The correct answer is C. The first half of the passage lays out the chain of specialists behind a single print—publisher, artist, carver, printer—and the second half observes that only the artist and publisher are usually named, while the carvers and printers, whose skill was decisive, remain anonymous. The structure is a description of shared labor followed by a point about unequal credit. Choice A introduces market value, which the passage never discusses. Choice B turns the passage into an argument about rival designers that it does not make. Choice D names a chemical process the passage does not describe.
